blocks.prompt: The Fish With No Bones
blocks.text: Every shark is a fish, but a shark is not built like other fish. Other fish have bones. A shark has none. Its whole body is held up by cartilage, the same bendy stuff inside your ears and your nose. Cartilage is light, so a shark can turn fast without getting tired. A shark's mouth is full of teeth, and behind those teeth are more teeth waiting in rows. When a tooth breaks, a new one slides forward to take its place. A shark can go through thousands of teeth in its life. Rub a shark the wrong way and its skin feels like sandpaper. It is covered in tiny scales shaped like little teeth.

blocks.prompt: Older Than Trees
blocks.text: Sharks were swimming in the ocean before there were trees on land. The first sharks appeared more than 400 million years ago. They were here before the dinosaurs, they were still here after the dinosaurs were gone, and they are here now. A shark is not like most other fish. It has no bones. Its skeleton is made of cartilage, the bendy material in your nose and your ears. Cartilage is much lighter than bone, which helps a shark stay up in the water without sinking. Most fish have a bag of air inside them, called a swim bladder, that keeps them afloat. Sharks do not have one. Instead a shark has a huge liver full of oil, and oil floats. Sharks come in surprising sizes. The whale shark is the biggest fish in the world. It can grow longer than a school bus, and it eats tiny drifting plankton. The dwarf lanternshark could sit in your hand, and it glows in the dark.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A shark's nostrils smell, they do not breathe
The lateral line feels movement in the water
Ampullae of Lorenzini sense electricity
It can find a flatfish buried in sand
Sharks breathe through gills, not nostrils

blocks.prompt: How a Shark Reads the Ocean
blocks.text: A shark hunts in water that is often dark, or cloudy, or both. Eyes alone would not be enough, so a shark reads the ocean with a whole set of senses, and some of them are senses you do not have. Start with smell. A shark's nostrils are not for breathing. A shark breathes through its gills. The nostrils do one job only: they sample the water. Seawater flows in one side and out the other, carrying scent with it, and a shark can pick up a trace of blood or fish oil spread thin through a great deal of water. People like to say a shark can smell a single drop of blood from miles away. That is an exaggeration, but the real ability is impressive enough. Next comes the lateral line, a row of tiny sensors running down each side of the body. It feels movement. A struggling fish pushes pressure waves out through the water, and the shark feels them arrive the way you might feel someone walking across a wooden floor. Then there is the strangest sense of all. Scattered across a shark's snout are small pores filled with jelly, called ampullae of Lorenzini. They detect electricity. Every living animal leaks a faint electrical field simply by moving its muscles and beating its heart, and a shark can sense that field. A flatfish buried under the sand is invisible and silent, but it cannot switch off its own heartbeat. In the final moments of a hunt, when the shark is close and, in some species, its eyes have rolled back for protection, electricity is what guides the bite. None of this makes a shark a monster. It makes it a very good reader. The ocean is full of signals, and sharks have had 400 million years of practice.

blocks.prompt: The Shark That Was Born Before Your Country
blocks.text: In the cold black water of the North Atlantic there lives a shark that does almost nothing quickly. The Greenland shark grows less than half an inch a year. It cruises at a pace a person could out-walk. Its flesh is loaded with chemicals that keep it from freezing in near-zero water, and those same chemicals make it poisonous to eat unless it is buried and fermented for months, which is exactly what Icelanders once learned to do. Many Greenland sharks carry a small parasite anchored to the surface of the eye, and a great number of them are effectively blind. In water this cold and this dark, sight was never worth much anyway. For a long time nobody knew how old these animals were. You cannot count growth rings in a shark's skeleton, because a shark has no bones to leave rings in. So researchers tried something clever. The lens at the center of an eye is built before birth and never replaced, which means the tissue at its core is exactly as old as the animal. By radiocarbon dating those cores, scientists estimated that the largest Greenland shark they measured was somewhere near 400 years old, and almost certainly older than 270. That makes it the longest-lived vertebrate we know of. A shark alive in the Arctic today may have been swimming while people were still writing with quill pens. There is a catch buried inside that number. A Greenland shark does not become old enough to have young of its own until it is roughly 150. A species that slow has no way to bounce back from being hunted, and thousands are still hauled up every year by accident, in nets set for other fish. This is the part of the shark story that usually gets told backward. People fear sharks. Sharks kill fewer than ten of us worldwide in a normal year. We kill somewhere near 80 million of them. The math is not close, and it never has been.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Shark That Never Stops Growing Teeth

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sharks predate the first forests
Skeleton is cartilage, never bone
Dermal denticles are built like teeth
Great whites are partly warm-bodied
More than 500 shark species
About a third of sharks and rays are threatened

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Predator in the Room
blocks.text: Sharks are older than trees. That sounds like a trick sentence, but the fossil record supports it. Recognizable sharks were hunting the oceans more than 400 million years ago, before the first forests took hold on land, before the dinosaurs arrived, and long before the dinosaurs left. Four mass extinctions have swept the planet since then. Sharks came through all four. Whatever a shark is doing, it works. Part of what it is doing is building itself cheaply. A shark has no bones. Its skeleton is cartilage, lighter and more flexible than bone, which lets a large animal stay agile without hauling a heavy frame around. Because a shark also lacks the gas-filled swim bladder that holds most fish at depth, it solves the floating problem with an enormous liver full of low-density oil. Its skin is not smooth, either. It is armored in dermal denticles, microscopic scales built from the same dentine and hard outer coating as its teeth, angled so that water slides past with less turbulence than it would over bare skin. A shark is, quite literally, wrapped in teeth. The teeth in its mouth are only the ones at the front of the line. Rows of replacements sit behind them inside the jaw, rotating forward as the working teeth snap off in use. A shark discards and rebuilds its bite continuously for its whole life. This is also why the fossil record is so tooth-heavy. Cartilage rots away, but teeth are mineral, and a single shark can leave thousands of them behind. None of this makes sharks one kind of animal. There are more than 500 species, and they behave nothing alike. The whale shark, the largest fish alive at up to about 60 feet, strains drifting plankton out of the water and could not harm you if it wanted to. The dwarf lanternshark fits in a human hand and glows. The cookiecutter shark, barely longer than your forearm, bites neat round plugs out of animals many times its size and swims away. The great white and its close relatives are partly warm-bodied, using dense bundles of blood vessels to trap the heat their swimming muscles produce and hold parts of the body well above the temperature of the sea around them, which is why they can hunt hard in cold water that would slow an ordinary fish to a crawl. And yet, in the story most people carry around, sharks are one thing: a threat. Here the numbers deserve a hearing. Worldwide, sharks bite roughly 60 to 80 people a year without being provoked, and about five to ten of those people die. Meanwhile, recent estimates put human killing of sharks near 80 million animals a year, many of them finned and dumped back over the side for a soup. Around a third of all shark and ray species are now threatened with extinction, and populations of open-ocean sharks and rays have fallen by more than seventy percent in fifty years. That collapse matters beyond the sharks themselves. Large sharks sit at the top of ocean food webs, and pulling a predator off the top of a food web does not leave the rest of it unchanged. Remove the animals that eat the animals that graze the reef, and the reef finds out. Four hundred million years is a long apprenticeship. The shark survived every catastrophe the planet could arrange on its own. The open question is whether it survives us, and that question is not really about the shark. It is about what we decide is worth keeping.
